newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Seagate pushes software in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Seagate pushes software in Asia.

text.p: Seagate Software is moving into Asia and the Pacific as part of a push to boost overseas revenue, a senior company official said on Friday.

"By the time we get to our goal in another two years from now, international revenue (outside North America) for Seagate Software worldwide should be in the 50-55 percent range," said Michel Montandon, vice president of international operations.
The company, a unit of Seagate Technology Inc, has said its revenue from software for data, storage and network management will likely reach about US$1.0 billion by 1999.
In the last financial quarter, Seagate had $55 million in software revenue, and annual revenue is projected to be about $250 million, Montandon told Reuters in an interview.

He said Singapore would be Seagate Software's regional hub and it would make use of its parent company's huge presence here. Seagate Technology has invested more than $1.1 billion in disk drive and other fixed asset investments in Singapore.

"We will start in a few markets where there is a huge NT servers market -- Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia -- and concentrate on these five markets in the next six to nine months," Montandon said.

Seagate was setting up sales, marketing and technical support services for these countries with initial investments of several million dollars. It would translate products into local languages and adapt them for local needs, Montandon said.
Its revenue from Asia-Pacific should grow rapidly, he said.

"Seagate Software in the Asia-Pacific region will grow at a minimum of 20 percent in terms of revenue and licences from one quarter over the next, so we can say it's way over 100 percent annual growth," in the first year, he said.

By comparison, software revenue from Europe grew more than 25 percent on a quarterly basis in the past three quarters and this was expected to continue. Europe contributes about 30 percent of the group's total revenue.
Growth in North America was below 20 percent quarterly, but this was about 65 percent of the company's total sales.
Seagate Software spent more than 20 percent of its revenue on research and development, higher than the industry norm. "This will continue for several more quarters," said Montandon.
He said its software gross margin stood at more than 80 percent and was profitable on a net level.
He declined to reveal net margins, but said the firm should be able to reach net margins of 25 percent before 1999.
In the longer term, Seagate would look at China and India. Plans for these emerging markets would be announced later in the year, he said without giving details.

He said Seagate Software was looking at a list of companies for licensing technology deals, to buy their products or for possible mergers. To reach its financial goal, Seagate needs to make at least one or two more major acquisitions before 2000.
